ruststream-gcp-pubsub is the Google Cloud Pub/Sub broker for RustStream, built on google-cloud-pubsub, the official client. The guides take a Pub/Sub service from installation to production. Start with Getting started.
This section draws how Google Cloud Pub/Sub works, where ruststream-gcp-pubsub sits between Pub/Sub and the RustStream runtime, and what that costs a service.
What ruststream-gcp-pubsub costs on every message: throughput against the raw google-cloud-pubsub client, and instructions and allocations of its code.

The first chart runs each scenario three ways against the local Pub/Sub emulator. Raw client drives google-cloud-pubsub directly. Broker crate drives this crate and nothing above it: its subscription, the deliveries it yields and its publisher, pulled and settled by a loop with no service around it. RustStream is the service a user writes: a #[subscriber] handler, the app and the runtime. The first gap is what this crate costs over the client it wraps, and it is the number this repository answers for. The second is what the runtime adds on top, over Pub/Sub in particular. Each loop is a bar from its best round to its slowest, with a dot at the best round and a notch at the median. The zero of the axis is the raw client's best round, and a dot right of zero is slower. A hollow dot is a loop whose difference from the raw client is smaller than the spread of the rounds. The table under the chart prints the best round with the median in parentheses. The second scenario publishes under ordering keys, the delivery shape a subscription with ordering enabled keeps in order per key. It also gives this crate one piece of work the first scenario does not have: the key is carried into the delivery's headers, where a service that names no broker reads it as a partition key. A loop on the client reads the field on the message and copies nothing.

The second chart counts what one message costs on the service's thread: instructions under callgrind and allocations under DHAT, in the steady state. Each scenario is the service a user writes, built on PubSubBroker and started against the emulator of the same stand. Everything on the service's thread is counted: the framework's dispatch, this crate's code and the google-cloud-pubsub client, whose streaming pull, acknowledgements, lease extensions and publish requests run there. Cold start is what starting the service and taking the first delivery cost once. Most of every row is the client. The reply row is the largest: the runtime waits for each reply to be confirmed before it takes the next delivery, so every reply leaves in a publish request of its own. The cold start is almost all the client too: it builds two administration clients, each of which reads and parses the machine's root certificates, so that column depends on the machine's certificate store.

How ruststream-gcp-pubsub measures itself: the three loops, the run against the emulator, the broker-bound arithmetic and the code count. The procedure is the framework's own (RustStream methodology), and this page states what it is on Pub/Sub.

One process runs each scenario three times over, as three loops that differ in one thing: what carries the messages. Raw client. google-cloud-pubsub, driven directly by a loop written by hand. Broker crate. This crate and nothing above it: its subscription, the deliveries it yields and its publisher, pulled and settled by a loop with no service around it. RustStream. The service a user writes: a #[subscriber] handler, the app and the runtime. Everything else is equal across the three: the endpoint and the credentials, the topology, the streaming-pull settings, the place of the ack, the decode into the same type, the payload bytes, the tokio runtime and the build. Every figure was taken against the local emulator that docker-compose.test.yml starts, and none of them against the hosted service.

The window opens at the first delivery and closes when the last one is settled, in every loop alike. The message count comes from a probe, which sets it so that every measured run lasts at least five seconds on whatever machine it is taken on. The loops are interleaved, three rounds. Each loop reports its best, median and worst round. A row is broker-bound when it was paced by the emulator. That is arithmetic: a probe outside the rounds times one round trip to the emulator, a delivery is charged one of them for its acknowledgement, and the row is flagged when that product covers at least half the time one message took. The round trip is published with the machine, so the arithmetic can be checked.

Each scenario of the cost chart is the service a user writes, built on PubSubBroker and started against the emulator of the same stand. The service runs on one thread, and everything on that thread is counted: the framework's dispatch, this crate's code and the google-cloud-pubsub client, whose streaming pull, acknowledgements, lease extensions and publish requests run there. The emulator is another process and is not in the number. The messages are published from another thread before the drain starts, and that work is not in the number either. Instructions come from callgrind and allocations from DHAT. Each is per message in the steady state: the slope between a run of 1000 deliveries and a run of 2000. The cold start is what starting the service and taking the first delivery cost once. The client acknowledges in batches and extends leases on timers, so a count moves a little from one run to the next: over five runs the instructions per message agreed within 5 percent, and the allocations of the longest run within 3,500 on the reply row and within 440 on the other two. just bench-code fails on an allocation above the floor a scenario declares: the highest count seen plus a margin at least as large as that spread, and a tenth of a percent at the least. With --baseline=main it also fails on more than two percent more instructions. A pull request that changes the cost cites its numbers.

just bench The recipe starts the emulator from docker-compose.test.yml, runs both scenarios, stops it again and rewrites docs/benchmarks/results.json with what it measured. It takes a few minutes and wants the machine to itself. It clears RUSTFLAGS, so the binary is not tied to the CPU it was built on. Both recipes build the benchmarks the way a release is built, with fat link-time optimization across crates, so the numbers describe the code a service ships. just bench-code The recipe starts the emulator, counts the code chart under valgrind, stops the emulator again and rewrites the code section of the same document. It takes a few minutes. Besides Docker it needs valgrind. The benchmark runner has to be the gungraun release Cargo.lock pins: the recipe installs it into target/ on its first run and again after the release changes. A number after the recipe name sets the deliveries per measured run (just bench-code 500); the published numbers are measured at the default of 1000. Any other argument goes to the benchmark runner, such as --save-baseline=main or --baseline=main. A run that breaches a limit still measures every scenario and prints the table. Every breached limit follows the table, with the value it was compared against next to the new one, and the run fails.
What the benchmark numbers of ruststream-gcp-pubsub measure, and what they do not allow you to conclude.

The three loops of a row are comparable with each other, because they ran in one process, interleaved, against one emulator. A row is not comparable with a row another broker crate publishes: the transports do different work per message. An overhead reported as indistinguishable is one where that loop and the raw client differ by less than the spread between runs of either. That is the honest outcome wherever the transport costs far more than the dispatch. A figure below the run-to-run noise would read as precision that was never measured, so none is published. A broker-bound row was paced by the emulator, so every loop spent the run in the same waiting. The difference between them is then a lower bound on what dispatch costs, not a measurement of it. The first row sits within a few percent of that line and crosses it from one run to the next, so whether it carries the flag says nothing about whether the consumer was ever the limit.

documents.t: The counts are absolute, the client's work and the framework's included; the core publishes the framework's cost alone on its benchmarks page. The same count costs more time where it misses the cache, so a count is not a time. Every figure is the steady state, the slope between a run of 1000 deliveries and one of 2000. Starting the service and taking the first delivery are the cold start, paid once.

The emulator is not the service. It answers the same API over plaintext on the loopback, and it leaves out the TLS handshake, the credential refresh and the round trip to a region. Every loop talks to the same emulator, so the comparison between them holds; the rate itself is a local number, and nothing here predicts what a subscription delivers from a region. Flow control is the other thing the emulator does not reproduce. It delivers as fast as it can, whatever limit the subscription carries, so no loop meets the pause a hosted subscription applies to a consumer that falls behind. A row is one consumer, one subscription, a small body and an emulator on the loopback. It measures what a delivery costs in this crate, not what Pub/Sub can carry. The numbers are a snapshot of one machine on one day, with the build recorded beside them. They are measured again by hand, on a machine given to the run alone: the differences they show are smaller than the noise of a shared one.

Everything Pub/Sub-specific is in this crate: the subscription descriptor, what each handler outcome does to a lease, and how a publish carries its ordering key. Connect builds four clients and shares them for the life of the connection: a Subscriber, a BasePublisher, a TopicAdmin and a SubscriptionAdmin. The admins create the topology a descriptor declares and write the dead-letter policy a registration declares. emulator points every client at a local emulator with anonymous credentials. Otherwise they use endpoint and credentials where given, and Application Default Credentials where not. Each subscription runs a pump task. It reads the client's stream and forwards each delivery into a channel of 16, which the runtime polls. Batches are assembled on that channel. The client's lease travels inside each PubSubMessage, so a settlement goes straight to the client. The publishers of a connection share one client publisher per topic, created on its first publish. The client batches what they send. Under the testing feature, TestApp connects the same broker to an in-process transport instead of the clients. It models topics and subscriptions, competing subscribers, acknowledgement and redelivery, attempt counting and dead-lettering. A build without the feature carries none of it. The pump task wraps it in a PubSubMessage without copying: the data stays the client's buffer, and the attributes move into the headers. The ordering key becomes the partition-key header, and the attempt count pubsub-delivery-attempt where the subscription has a dead-letter policy. The handler's reply is encoded into a buffer that becomes the outgoing message's data as it is, because the client keeps the bytes it publishes. The headers become attributes; a header that is not UTF-8 fails the publish, because an attribute is text. A key named for the publish becomes the message's ordering key, as Ordered delivery draws. The publish returns once the service has assigned the message an id. A reply that fails to publish settles the delivery with a retry, so the message comes back. The delivery settles after the reply. An ack leaves with the client's next batch of acknowledgements, within about 100 milliseconds. What each outcome becomes is on Settlement.

The model is Google's (subscription overview, Pub/Sub basics). How a subscriber holds a message while it works is on Leases.

A streaming pull leases each message: the client extends its ack deadline while the handler works, and flow control caps how many it holds. A streaming pull: messages arrive under a lease the client extends while the application holds them, and acks go back in batchesmessagesextendssettledack, nackgoogle-cloud-pubsubApplicationPub/Sub subscriptionan ack deadline per messageStreaming pullup to max_outstandingLease setchecked every 3 sAcks andnacks, sentin batchesevery 100 msHandlerholds the messageSettles it:ack or nackPast max_lease the client stops extending:the deadline runs out and the message comes back The diagram as text google-cloud-pubsub: Streaming pull up to max_outstanding; Lease set checked every 3 s; Acks and nacks, sent in batches every 100 ms Application: Handler holds the message; Settles it: ack or nack Pub/Sub subscription an ack deadline per message → Streaming pull up to max_outstanding: messages Streaming pull up to max_outstanding → Lease set checked every 3 s Lease set checked every 3 s → Handler holds the message Handler holds the message → Settles it: ack or nack Lease set checked every 3 s → Pub/Sub subscription an ack deadline per message: extends Settles it: ack or nack → Acks and nacks, sent in batches every 100 ms: settled Acks and nacks, sent in batches every 100 ms → Pub/Sub subscription an ack deadline per message: ack, nack Past max_lease the client stops extending: the deadline runs out and the message comes back A streaming pull is one long-lived gRPC stream per subscription. The service sends messages down it as they arrive, and each one comes with an ack deadline. A message that is neither acknowledged nor extended before its deadline is delivered again, possibly to another subscriber. The client library holds that deadline off. It sends modifyAckDeadline for every message the application still holds, pushing each deadline at most ack_extension ahead (60 seconds by default, clamped to 10 to 600). It does so for at most max_lease, one hour by default. A process that dies sends no extensions, so its messages return to the subscription once their deadlines pass. Flow control is on the stream. The service stops sending while max_outstanding messages (1000 by default) or 100 MiB are unsettled on it, and resumes when the count drops below. A slow handler therefore slows its own stream down, and the messages it has not received wait in the subscription. An ack removes the message from the subscription. A nack is a modifyAckDeadline with a deadline of zero: the message leaves the lease set, and the service delivers it again, as Redelivery draws. The figures are the google-cloud-pubsub 1.3 client's (Subscribe) and Google's (lease management).

Messages that share an ordering key, published in one region, reach a subscription with message ordering in the order they were published. Two ordering keys from one publisher: each key is published one batch at a time and delivered in its own orderin key orderSubscription with message orderingPublisherone batch in flight per keyKey order-1:#1, #2, #3Key order-2:#1, #2Topicpublished to in one regionorder-1:#1, then #2,then #3order-2:#1, then #2A redelivery of order-1 #2 brings #3 back too,even when #3 was acknowledged The diagram as text Subscription with message ordering: order-1: #1, then #2, then #3; order-2: #1, then #2 Publisher one batch in flight per key → Key order-1: #1, #2, #3 Publisher one batch in flight per key → Key order-2: #1, #2 Key order-1: #1, #2, #3 → Topic published to in one region Key order-2: #1, #2 → Topic published to in one region Topic published to in one region → Subscription with message ordering: in key order A redelivery of order-1 #2 brings #3 back too, even when #3 was acknowledged Order holds per key and nowhere else. Messages of different keys, and messages without a key, arrive in any order. Ordering is a property of the subscription, set when it is created and fixed after that. A subscription without it delivers keyed messages in any order. The client publisher keeps one batch in flight per key, so a key's messages reach the service in the order the application published them. Messages without a key are sent concurrently. A failed publish pauses its key: the client refuses that key's later messages until the application resumes it. The service orders what it receives in one region. Publishers of one key in several regions get no order between them, and a regional endpoint (endpoint) keeps them in one. Subscribers may connect from anywhere. Messages of one key usually go to the same subscriber of the subscription, but the service may move a key to another subscriber. A key is at most 1 KB, and one key publishes at most 1 MBps. With a dead-letter policy on the subscription, the order may not hold, because dead-lettering is best effort.

A publish takes its key from the call's ordering_key step first, then from a partition-key header, then from the key the PubSubPublish policy fixed at the mount site. The key travels as the message's ordering key, never as an attribute. When a keyed publish fails, the crate resumes the key and returns the error, so the next publish under that key is sent. A delivery reports its key as the partition-key header. Keyed worker lanes (workers(n, by_key)) hash it, so one key keeps its order inside the service too. The subscription the crate creates through create_with_topic has message ordering on. A subscription it finds keeps its own setting. The rules are Google's (ordering messages); the publisher's are the google-cloud-pubsub 1.3 client's (Publisher).

Pub/Sub delivers a message again after a nack or an expired deadline, until a dead-letter policy moves it to a dead-letter topic. One delivery on Pub/Sub: an ack removes the message, a nack or an expired deadline brings it back until the dead-letter capbelowat the capA delivery of one messagedelivery_attempt: nack:removed fromthe subscriptionnack, or thedeadline expiresDead-letter policy:is n belowmaxDeliveryAttempts?At the cap:published to thedead-letter topicBelow the cap, orno policy: the retrypolicy waits, thenit comes backThe attempt count is approximateand can reset to zero The diagram as text A delivery of one message delivery_attempt: n → ack: removed from the subscription A delivery of one message delivery_attempt: n → nack, or the deadline expires nack, or the deadline expires → Dead-letter policy: is n below maxDeliveryAttempts? Dead-letter policy: is n below maxDeliveryAttempts? → Below the cap, or no policy: the retry policy waits, then it comes back: below Dead-letter policy: is n below maxDeliveryAttempts? → At the cap: published to the dead-letter topic: at the cap Below the cap, or no policy: the retry policy waits, then it comes back → A delivery of one message delivery_attempt: n The attempt count is approximate and can reset to zero A subscription redelivers at once by default. Its retry policy can add an exponential backoff instead, between 0 and 600 seconds (10 and 600 by default). The backoff is best effort: under many nacks a message may wait less. A dead-letter policy is a property of the subscription: a dead-letter topic and maxDeliveryAttempts, from 5 to 100 (5 by default). Only a subscription with one counts attempts, and only then does a delivery carry delivery_attempt. Because forwarding is best effort, a message may be delivered a few more times than the cap. The service moves a message by publishing it to the dead-letter topic and acknowledging it in the subscription. Its service agent needs the publisher role on that topic and the subscriber role on the subscription. A dead-letter topic with no subscription of its own loses what it receives.

Exactly-once delivery is another property of the subscription, for pull and streaming pull. An ack the service confirms is final: the message is not delivered again. The client must ask for that confirmation, and the guarantee holds only for subscribers that connect in the same region, which a regional endpoint ensures. Its deliveries take noticeably longer than on a standard subscription.

A delivery reports delivery_attempt as the pubsub-delivery-attempt header. A registration's max_attempts(n) and dead_letter(topic) become the subscription's dead-letter policy, written when the subscription opens. A cap outside 5 to 100, or one of the two declared without the other, fails the start before any call to the service. How each handler outcome reaches this picture is on Settlement. The rules are Google's (retry policy, dead-letter topics, exactly-once delivery).

What ack, retry, retry_after and drop become on Pub/Sub, which acknowledges, rejects or keeps leasing each message. The exception is the last delivery the subscription's dead-letter policy allows. There a nack is what moves the message to the dead-letter topic, so drop() nacks. The crate reads the attempt from the delivery. The cap comes from the registration's max_attempts(n), or from the subscription itself, read once at startup, when an operator set the policy outside the code. That read needs the pubsub.subscriptions.get permission; without it the service logs a warning and drop() acknowledges. The attempt count is approximate, so a count that reset makes drop() acknowledge too. A decode failure drops the message by default (FailurePolicy), so on Pub/Sub it is acknowledged. The subscription counts attempts and moves spent messages itself. retry() under a declared max_attempts is a nack like any other, and the service applies the cap. The runtime publishes no retry copy on this broker. retry_after(d) keeps the delivery in the process. A task on the runtime the broker connected on waits for d and then nacks. Meanwhile the client goes on extending the lease, and the message counts against max_outstanding. A d longer than max_lease is refused at the call with PubSubError::DelayBeyondLease, because the lease would end first. If the process dies during the wait, the lease ends and the service delivers the message again: the delay is lost, the message is not. On an exactly-once subscription the crate uses the client's confirmed ack and nack. An ack that returns has been accepted by the service, and a refused one is logged as a failed ack. On any other subscription an ack is best effort, and the message may still come back.

The parts of ruststream-gcp-pubsub a Pub/Sub service uses: the broker (PubSubBroker), its subscription descriptor (GooglePubSub), its publish policy (PubSubPublish) and the in-process transport a TestApp test runs on.

With the asyncapi feature the generated document speaks googlepubsub: the server's host and the ordering key a mount site fixed. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. This crate adds what it knows about Pub/Sub to the parts the core writes. A server reports the host clients dial, under the protocol googlepubsub. A message carries the specification's googlepubsub binding, version 0.2.0, where its mount site fixed an ordering key. The channels are the subscriptions the service reads and the topics it publishes to. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker and the publish policies. The document is published and shared, so no part of it carries a credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-gcp-pubsub = { version = "0.7", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label pubsub, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example pubsub_asyncapi --features asyncapi -- asyncapi gen prints the document. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: PubSubBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "1.0.0")).with_broker_labeled("pubsub", broker, |b| { // Every receipt goes out under one key, so the document states it. b.include(receipt) .out_reply(Publish::default().ordering_key("receipts")); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker()) } examples/manual/pubsub_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: PubSubBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "1.0.0")).with_broker_labeled("pubsub", broker, |b| { // Every receipt goes out under one key, so the document states it. b.include(subscriber(orders(), ReceiptFor).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default().ordering_key("receipts")); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker()) }

A subscription is a channel the service receives on, and a topic a channel it sends to; neither carries a googlepubsub binding. A channel the service receives on is named after the subscription. The topic behind a subscription is a fact of the service's infrastructure, which the document, built before anything connects, does not see. A channel the service publishes to reports the topic the mount site resolved as its address: a reply type's #[outgoing(name)], a reply("dest") clause, or a slot's destination. The channel binding of googlepubsub describes a topic's configuration: labels, retention, storage policy and schema. No descriptor or publish policy holds those, so channels carry no binding.

The subscription orders-workers is a channel the service receives on, and the topic receipts one it sends to. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_asyncapi.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` is a channel the service receives on, and the topic /// `receipts` a channel it sends to. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers"), reply)] async fn receipt(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id } } examples/manual/pubsub_asyncapi.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` is a channel the service receives on, and the topic /// `receipts` a channel it sends to. struct ReceiptFor; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for ReceiptFor { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } fn orders() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers") }

A publish policy with a fixed ordering key writes it into the googlepubsub binding of the message the mount site sends. The message binding of googlepubsub describes what a message carries beyond its payload and attributes. This crate fills orderingKey where the mount site's policy fixed one. A key named per message, by the ordering_key step or the partition-key header, is named at a call site, which the document does not see. A message whose mount site fixed no key carries no binding.

Every receipt goes out under the key receipts. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: PubSubBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "1.0.0")).with_broker_labeled("pubsub", broker, |b| { // Every receipt goes out under one key, so the document states it. b.include(receipt) .out_reply(Publish::default().ordering_key("receipts")); }) } examples/manual/pubsub_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: PubSubBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "1.0.0")).with_broker_labeled("pubsub", broker, |b| { // Every receipt goes out under one key, so the document states it. b.include(subscriber(orders(), ReceiptFor).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default().ordering_key("receipts")); }) } The message Receipt in the document: { "googlepubsub": { "orderingKey": "receipts", "bindingVersion": "0.2.0" } }

The server reports the host and port clients dial under the protocol googlepubsub, never a scheme, a path or credentials. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its host is the emulator address where one is set, the endpoint where one is set, and pubsub.googleapis.com otherwise. A scheme, a path and any user info the endpoint carries stay out of it. The protocol is googlepubsub. protocolVersion stays out, and the server has no binding: the specification's googlepubsub binding describes no server field.

The broker reaches the regional endpoint, and its server in the document is us-east1-pubsub.googleapis.com. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_asyncapi.rs /// The regional endpoint; the document reports `us-east1-pubsub.googleapis.com`. fn broker() -> PubSubBroker { PubSubBroker::new("my-project").endpoint("https://us-east1-pubsub.googleapis.com") } examples/manual/pubsub_asyncapi.rs /// The regional endpoint; the document reports `us-east1-pubsub.googleapis.com`. fn broker() -> PubSubBroker { PubSubBroker::new("my-project").endpoint("https://us-east1-pubsub.googleapis.com") }

PubSubBroker connects a service to Google Cloud Pub/Sub; new only records the project, and the runtime connects it at startup. PubSubBroker::new takes the project id that short topic and subscription names resolve in. It does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. The settings that follow it are builder steps too: a local emulator, explicit credentials and another service endpoint. Without them the broker reaches pubsub.googleapis.com with Application Default Credentials. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedPubSubBroker. Every subscription and every publisher of the service opens against that connected form. At shutdown the runtime flushes what the service published and closes the connection. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] reads the existing subscription orders-workers of the project. A name is a short id or a full resource name, projects/{project}/subscriptions/{id}. Every other setting of a subscription belongs to the GooglePubSub descriptor.

The service reads the subscription orders-workers of the project my-project. cargo run --example pubsub_broker --features testing -- run starts it against Pub/Sub. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_broker.rs /// Reads the subscription `orders-workers`. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Application Default Credentials, against `pubsub.googleapis.com`. #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(place); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_broker.rs /// Reads the subscription `orders-workers`. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Application Default Credentials, against `pubsub.googleapis.com`. fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders-workers", Place).build()); }, ) }

credentials replaces Application Default Credentials with a credentials value built by google-cloud-auth. By default every client of the broker authenticates with Application Default Credentials. They come from GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, the file gcloud auth application-default login writes, or the metadata server of the machine the service runs on. credentials takes a Credentials value instead. The google-cloud-auth crate builds one from a service account key, an impersonated service account, or an external account. The value only records how to obtain a token; the clients ask for one when they call the service. Startup does not read the credentials, so wrong credentials surface on the first call, as an error of the subscription or the publish.

The deployment mounts a service account key as a secret, and the broker signs in with it. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_broker_config.rs /// Signs in with the service account key the deployment mounts as a secret. fn broker(key: Value) -> Result<PubSubBroker, CredentialsError> { let credentials = service_account::Builder::new(key).build()?; Ok(PubSubBroker::new("my-project").credentials(credentials)) } examples/manual/pubsub_broker_config.rs /// Signs in with the service account key the deployment mounts as a secret. fn broker(key: Value) -> Result<PubSubBroker, CredentialsError> { let credentials = service_account::Builder::new(key).build()?; Ok(PubSubBroker::new("my-project").credentials(credentials)) }

emulator(address) points every client of the broker at a local Pub/Sub emulator, with anonymous credentials. The address is either a host:port, which the broker dials over plaintext, or a URL such as http://localhost:8085, which it dials as written. The Google client libraries for Rust do not read PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST, so the address is a setting of the broker. With an emulator set, the endpoint and the credentials steps have no effect. The emulator accepts any project id and starts empty. A subscription that creates itself with create_with_topic is the usual form against it. The emulator keeps its topics and subscriptions until it stops, so a second run finds what the first one created. The repository's stand is docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts on port 8085.

The service runs against the emulator at localhost:8085. Its test runs the same service in process, and against the emulator when PUBSUB_TEST_HOST names one. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_broker_emulator.rs /// The emulator at `host`, a `host:port` without a scheme. fn broker(host: &str) -> PubSubBroker { PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator(host) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("localhost:8085")) } examples/manual/pubsub_broker_emulator.rs /// The emulator at `host`, a `host:port` without a scheme. fn broker(host: &str) -> PubSubBroker { PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator(host) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker("localhost:8085")) }

endpoint names another Pub/Sub endpoint, such as a locational endpoint that keeps every request of the service in one region. By default the broker reaches the global endpoint, https://pubsub.googleapis.com. A locational endpoint, such as https://us-east1-pubsub.googleapis.com, routes every request to that region. Two Pub/Sub guarantees hold only inside one region. Messages that share an ordering key arrive in order when they are published to the same region. An exactly-once subscription guarantees one delivery to subscribers that connect in the region of the subscription. The endpoint applies to every client of the broker: subscriptions, publishers and the topology calls at startup. The AsyncAPI server reports the endpoint's host.

Every request of the service goes to us-east1. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_broker_config.rs /// The regional endpoint of `us-east1`: every request of the service goes to that region. fn regional() -> PubSubBroker { PubSubBroker::new("my-project").endpoint("https://us-east1-pubsub.googleapis.com") } examples/manual/pubsub_broker_config.rs /// The regional endpoint of `us-east1`: every request of the service goes to that region. fn regional() -> PubSubBroker { PubSubBroker::new("my-project").endpoint("https://us-east1-pubsub.googleapis.com") }

PubSubError is the one error type of the crate: connect, admin, receive, publish, not connected, invalid descriptor and a delay past the lease. Each variant names the step that failed. The client library's error behind it is its source, so the library's types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect a client could not be built Admin a topic or subscription call at startup failed, such as a create without permission Receive a streaming pull failed for good, such as a subscription that does not exist Publish the service refused a message, or the crate refused one it cannot send, such as an attribute that is not UTF-8 NotConnected a publisher was used after the broker shut down InvalidDescriptor a subscription the crate cannot open: an empty name, half a dead-letter declaration, a cap outside 5 to 100 DelayBeyondLease a retry_after asked for more than the subscription's max_lease A service meets the error in three places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. A settlement the subscription refuses, such as a delay past the lease, reaches the runtime as the source of an AckError. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

A shipment whose note exceeds the 1024 bytes an attribute holds is refused; the handler logs the cause and drops the order. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_broker_errors.rs /// Ships an order with its note as an attribute of the shipment. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("note", order.note.clone()); let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; if let Err(err) = out.message(&shipment).with_headers(headers).publish().await { // The error names the topic and the service's reason. The same shipment would be // refused again, so the order is dropped rather than retried. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders-workers", order.id, error = %err, "shipment refused"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_broker_errors.rs /// Ships an order with its note as an attribute of the shipment. struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("note", order.note.clone()); let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&shipment) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { // The error names the topic and the service's reason. The same shipment would be // refused again, so the order is dropped rather than retried. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders-workers", order.id, error = %err, "shipment refused"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } }

One glob, ruststream_gcp_pubsub::prelude, brings the core prelude, the broker, the descriptor, the publish policy and the ordering step. use ruststream_gcp_pubsub::prelude::*; is the one import a Pub/Sub service writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds PubSubBroker, the descriptor GooglePubSub and the live PubSubPublisher. The publish policy comes under the name every broker crate uses: Publish is PubSubPublish. So a mount site reads the same on every broker. Two broker preludes in one file collide on this name; the prefixed type at the crate root tells them apart. A handler body bounds its slots with capability traits, such as Out<impl Publisher>, and names no broker type. The one exception is a body that names an ordering key on one publish. The ordering_key step needs PubSubOrdering in scope and the slot bounded Out<impl Publisher<Options = PubSubPublishOptions>>, both from this prelude. The constants PARTITION_KEY_HEADER and DELIVERY_ATTEMPT_HEADER stay at the crate root.

The descriptor, the broker and the reply policy all come from the one glob. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_broker_prelude.rs /// The descriptor, the broker and the policy all come from the one glob. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").create_with_topic("orders"), reply)] async fn receipt(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(receipt).out_reply(Publish::default()); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_broker_prelude.rs /// The descriptor, the broker and the policy all come from the one glob. struct ReceiptFor; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for ReceiptFor { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").create_with_topic("orders"), ReceiptFor, ) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish::default()); }, ) }

Shutdown flushes every message the service still buffers; a publisher used afterwards reports PubSubError::NotConnected. The client library sends published messages in batches, so a publish may wait in a buffer for a few milliseconds. At shutdown the runtime stops the subscriptions and closes the connection, then flushes the buffer of every topic the service published to. A message published before the shutdown reaches the topic before the service exits. A subscription that stops ends its streaming pull; the deliveries the service has not settled come back to the subscription once their leases run out. A publisher taken before the shutdown keeps pointing at the closed connection. A publish through it returns PubSubError::NotConnected and never succeeds against the dead connection.

The handler replies with a shipment, and the shipment reaches its topic before the service exits. Its test publishes through a publisher taken before the start and gets NotConnected after the shutdown. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_broker_shutdown.rs /// Answers every order with a shipment on the topic `shipments`. #[subscriber("orders-workers", reply)] async fn ship(order: &Order) -> Shipment { Shipment { order_id: order.id } } fn service(broker: PubSubBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { // At shutdown the runtime flushes the shipments still buffered for `shipments`. At startup the broker builds its clients, then each subscription creates or updates its topology and opens a streaming pull. The runtime connects the broker once, after the synchronous builder has run. The connect builds four clients of the Google client library: a subscriber, a publisher, and the topic and subscription admin clients. The clients open their connections on first use. Then each subscription opens in turn. A descriptor the service cannot express fails the startup before any call: an empty name, or a dead-letter declaration with one half missing or a cap outside 5 to 100. A descriptor with create_with_topic creates its topic, its dead-letter topic and the subscription where they are missing. A subscription that already exists and carries a dead-letter declaration gets the declared policy written onto it. Each of these calls needs the matching Pub/Sub permission, and a refusal fails the startup with PubSubError::Admin. Last, the subscription opens its streaming pull. A subscription that does not exist fails there, on its stream, with PubSubError::Receive.

The subscription orders-workers creates itself on the topic orders with a dead-letter policy of five attempts. Its test also starts the same service with a cap of three, which the startup refuses. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_broker_startup.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` on the topic `orders`, both created when they are missing. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").create_with_topic("orders"))] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // Before the pull opens: the topics `orders` and `orders-dead`, then the // subscription with its dead-letter policy. b.include(place) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("orders-dead"); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_broker_startup.rs struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The subscription `orders-workers` on the topic `orders`, both created when they are missing. fn orders() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").create_with_topic("orders") } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // Before the pull opens: the topics `orders` and `orders-dead`, then the // subscription with its dead-letter policy. b.include(subscriber(orders(), Place).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("orders-dead"); }, ) }

PubSubPublish, Publish in the prelude, is the publish policy; every publish waits for the message id Pub/Sub assigns. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into a PubSubPublisher. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through this one. The destination is a topic, a short id in the broker's project or a full resource name. A reply goes to the topic its type names, and a slot publish to the topic the call or the slot names. The encoded message becomes the Pub/Sub message's data without a copy, and headers become its attributes. The client library keeps one publisher per topic, created on first use, which sends messages in batches of up to 100 messages, 1 MB or 10 milliseconds. A publish returns once the service has accepted the message and assigned its id, or with the error it reported as PubSubError::Publish. The policy's one setting is a default ordering key.

A reply goes to the topic of its type, and an invoice to the topic the call names. match out.message(&invoice).to("invoices").publish().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, error = %err, "invoice not published"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing.rs /// The invoice goes to the topic the call names. struct Bill; let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&invoice) .to("invoices") .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(order.id, error = %err, "invoice not published"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); Headers travel as Pub/Sub attributes, with no envelope of their own; an attribute that is not UTF-8 fails the publish. Every header of an outgoing message becomes an attribute of the Pub/Sub message, name and value unchanged. Each attribute of a delivery becomes a header, so a handler reads it with ctx.headers(). Attributes are text, so a header value that is not UTF-8 fails the publish with PubSubError::Publish instead of being rewritten. Pub/Sub accepts at most 100 attributes per message, names of up to 256 bytes and values of up to 1024 bytes, and refuses a message past them. Two headers have a meaning of their own. partition-key is the message's ordering key: it never travels as an attribute, and a delivery reports its ordering key under it. pubsub-delivery-attempt is the attempt number a delivery reports where the subscription counts attempts.

The tenant arrives as an attribute of the order and leaves as an attribute of the shipment. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_headers.rs /// The tenant arrives as an attribute of the order and leaves as an attribute of the shipment. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] async fn ship( order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); if let Some(tenant) = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant") { headers.insert("tenant", tenant.to_owned()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; match out.message(&shipment).with_headers(headers).publish().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_headers.rs /// The tenant arrives as an attribute of the order and leaves as an attribute of the shipment. struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); if let Some(tenant) = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant") { headers.insert("tenant", tenant.to_owned()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&shipment) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

On a subscription with message ordering, messages that share an ordering key reach a subscriber in the order they were published. An ordering key is a string a publish carries, up to 1 KB. A subscription orders deliveries only when it was created with message ordering on, a setting that cannot change afterwards. A subscription create_with_topic creates has it on; one created elsewhere keeps its own setting. The order holds for messages of one key published to one region, so publishers of one key use the same locational endpoint. When a message of a key is redelivered, the messages published after it under that key come again too, acknowledged ones included. With a dead-letter policy on the subscription, the order may not hold. A publish names its key in one of three places, and the first one present wins. The ordering_key step, or a transform, writes it into the message's settings. The partition-key header is the portable spelling. The policy's default key applies where neither named one. A delivery reports the key it arrived under in the partition-key header.

Three events of one order, published under its key, arrive in that order. The test runs the same body in process and against the emulator. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_ordering.rs /// The subscription `create_with_topic` creates has message ordering on, so the events of one /// order arrive in the order they were published. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("ordering-order-events-workers").create_with_topic("ordering-order-events") )] async fn track(event: &OrderEvent, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let key = ctx .headers() .get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) .unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(event.order_id, event.step, key, "order event"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_ordering.rs /// The subscription `create_with_topic` creates has message ordering on, so the events of one /// order arrive in the order they were published. struct Track; impl Handle<OrderEvent> for Track { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let key = ctx .headers() .get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) .unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(event.order_id, event.step, key, "order event"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn order_events() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("ordering-order-events-workers").create_with_topic("ordering-order-events") }

The ordering_key step names the ordering key of one publish, on the framework's publish builder. The step sits between message(..) and publish(), so the publish stays the mount site's: its codec, its transforms and its slot hold. It exists only on a builder over a Pub/Sub publisher. The handler bounds its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = PubSubPublishOptions>> and imports the prelude, which brings the PubSubOrdering trait. The key reaches the client as the message's own ordering key and never as an attribute. A key named by the call wins over the partition-key header and over the policy's key. A test reads the setting back with tb.out::<Slot>().with_options(..) and a PubSubPublishOptions value.

Each confirmation goes out under its order's key. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_ordering_key.rs /// Each confirmation goes out under its order's key, named on the call. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] async fn confirm( order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher<Options = PubSubPublishOptions>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let sent = out .message(&Confirmation { order_id: order.id }) .to("confirmations") .ordering_key(format!("order-{}", order.id)) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_ordering_key.rs /// Each confirmation goes out under its order's key, named on the call. struct Confirm; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Confirm where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher<Options = PubSubPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&Confirmation { order_id: order.id }) .to("confirmations") .ordering_key(format!("order-{}", order.id)) .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

The partition-key header is the portable spelling of the ordering key, read on publish and written on every keyed delivery. A body that names no broker type sets the key through this header. On publish the header becomes the message's ordering key and does not travel as an attribute. The header names the same key as the in-memory broker's partition-key, so a service keeps its headers when it moves between the two. A key from the ordering_key step or a transform wins over the header, and the header wins over the policy's key. A value that is not UTF-8 fails the publish. On a delivery the header holds the key the message was published under, and it is absent on a message without one.

The handler sets the header, and the shipment goes out under the order's key. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_ordering_header.rs /// The body names no broker type: the `partition-key` header orders the shipment. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, format!("order-{}", order.id)); let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = out .message(&shipment) .with_headers(headers) .to("shipments") .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_ordering_header.rs /// The body names no broker type: the `partition-key` header orders the shipment. struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, format!("order-{}", order.id)); let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&shipment) .with_headers(headers) .to("shipments") .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

Publish::default().ordering_key(..) orders every message of one mount site under one key, a reply included. The key belongs to the policy, so it applies to every publish of that slot or reply. A reply has no call site, so the policy is where a fixed key for replies goes. It suits a slot that belongs to one entity: one ledger, one device. A key named by the call or by the partition-key header wins over it. The AsyncAPI document reports the key in the message's binding.

Every ledger entry goes out under the key ledger. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_ordering_policy.rs /// Books every order in the ledger. #[subscriber("orders-workers", reply)] async fn book(order: &Order) -> LedgerEntry { LedgerEntry { order_id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // The ledger is one sequence, so every entry goes out under one key. b.include(book) .out_reply(Publish::default().ordering_key("ledger")); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_ordering_policy.rs /// Books every order in the ledger. struct Book; impl Handle<Order, LedgerEntry> for Book { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LedgerEntry, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(LedgerEntry { order_id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // The ledger is one sequence, so every entry goes out under one key. b.include(subscriber("orders-workers", Book).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default().ordering_key("ledger")); }, ) }

A reply transform over PubSubPublishOptions sets the reply's ordering key per delivery, read off the request. A reply has no call site, so a key that differs per reply is a transform's to write. The transform implements PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, PubSubPublishOptions> and reads the delivery being answered. It writes the key into the message's settings, where the ordering_key step would. Naming the settings type ties the transform to Pub/Sub publishers: it mounts on no other broker. The mount site adds it after the reply policy with .transform(..).

Each receipt goes out under the key of the order it answers. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_ordering_transform.rs /// Sends each receipt under the key of the order it answers, which the delivery reports in its /// `partition-key` header. struct ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey; impl<C> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, PubSubPublishOptions> for ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, _out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, options: &mut Option<PubSubPublishOptions>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(key) = cx.headers().get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) { options .get_or_insert_with(PubSubPublishOptions::default) .ordering_key = Some(key.to_owned()); } } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(receipt) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_ordering_transform.rs /// Sends each receipt under the key of the order it answers, which the delivery reports in its /// `partition-key` header. struct ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey; impl<C> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, PubSubPublishOptions> for ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, _out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, options: &mut Option<PubSubPublishOptions>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(key) = cx.headers().get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) { options .get_or_insert_with(PubSubPublishOptions::default) .ordering_key = Some(key.to_owned()); } } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders-workers", ReceiptFor).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey); }, ) }

ack acknowledges a delivery, retry nacks it so Pub/Sub redelivers it, and drop acknowledges one that is not worth another attempt. Pub/Sub settles each message on its own, by acknowledging it or by giving it back. ack acknowledges, and the subscription does not deliver the message again. retry nacks, and the subscription redelivers the message, possibly to another consumer. A subscription with no retry policy redelivers at once; one with an exponential backoff policy waits first. drop acknowledges too: Pub/Sub has no verb that discards a message without settling it. The one exception is the last delivery a dead-letter policy allows: there drop nacks, so the service moves the message to the dead-letter topic. A delayed retry is retry_after.

A subscription with exactly-once delivery on guarantees that an acknowledged message is not delivered again. It is a property of the subscription's configuration, and the crate reads it off each delivery. On such a subscription an ack and a nack wait for the service to confirm them. An acknowledgement the service rejects, such as one whose lease has expired, fails the settlement with an AckError that carries the cause, and the message may come back. On other subscriptions an ack is sent in the background and returns at once. The guarantee holds for subscribers in the subscription's region, which a locational endpoint pins.

A reservation acknowledges an order it reserved, drops an order with nothing to reserve, and asks for another delivery while the stock is out. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_settlement.rs /// Reserves stock for an order. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").create_with_topic("orders"))] async fn reserve(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.quantity == 0 { // Nothing to reserve, now or later: acknowledged, never redelivered. return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } if !order.in_stock { // Nacked: the subscription delivers the order again. return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, "stock reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_settlement.rs /// Reserves stock for an order. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Order> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.quantity == 0 { // Nothing to reserve, now or later: acknowledged, never redelivered. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } if !order.in_stock { // Nacked: the subscription delivers the order again. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(order.id, "stock reserved"); ready(Ok(())) } }

On a subscription with a dead-letter policy a delivery reports its attempt number in the pubsub-delivery-attempt header. Pub/Sub counts the deliveries of a message only where its subscription has a dead-letter policy. There each delivery carries the count, the first delivery being attempt 1, and the crate puts it in the header pubsub-delivery-attempt. A subscription without a policy reports no count, and the header is absent. A handler reads it with ctx.headers().get_str(DELIVERY_ATTEMPT_HEADER) and branches on it, for example to give a message up before the cap. The count is the service's estimate: it may miss a delivery, and it may start over from zero. The crate also reads it to tell the last allowed delivery, where drop nacks instead of acknowledging.

An order without stock waits through two redeliveries and is given up on the third attempt, before the cap of five. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_settlement_attempts.rs /// Waits for stock through two redeliveries, then gives the order up on the third attempt. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").create_with_topic("orders"))] async fn reserve(order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let attempt: u32 = ctx .headers() .get_str(DELIVERY_ATTEMPT_HEADER) .and_then(|attempt| attempt.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if order.in_stock { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } if attempt >= 3 { tracing::error!(order.id, attempt, "no stock, order given up"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::warn!(order.id, attempt, "no stock yet"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } examples/manual/pubsub_settlement_attempts.rs /// Waits for stock through two redeliveries, then gives the order up on the third attempt. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Order> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let attempt: u32 = ctx .headers() .get_str(DELIVERY_ATTEMPT_HEADER) .and_then(|attempt| attempt.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if order.in_stock { return ready(Ok(())); } if attempt >= 3 { tracing::error!(order.id, attempt, "no stock, order given up"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::warn!(order.id, attempt, "no stock yet"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())) } }

max_attempts(n) and dead_letter(topic) at the mount site become the subscription's own dead-letter policy, written at startup. A Pub/Sub subscription moves a spent message itself. After n deliveries the service stops redelivering the message and publishes it to the dead-letter topic, with its payload and its attributes. The crate publishes nothing: it writes the declaration onto the subscription as its dead-letter policy. A subscription that create_with_topic creates carries the policy from the start, and the dead-letter topic is created with it. A subscription that already exists gets the policy written onto it at startup, whether the handler names it by string or by descriptor. The policy is one field of the subscription with both halves, so the mount site declares both. A cap without a topic, a topic without a cap, or a cap outside the 5 to 100 Pub/Sub accepts fails the startup. Two registrations on one subscription that declare different policies fail the startup too. .out_retry(..) does not compile on this broker, because no retry copy is ever published. The dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic, read through a subscription of its own. A message published to a topic with no subscription is lost, so the reader's subscription exists before the first message is spent. The Pub/Sub service account of the project needs permission to publish to the dead-letter topic and to subscribe to the source subscription. Pub/Sub counts deliveries on a best-effort basis, so a message may get a few more or fewer than n.

Five deliveries of a declined payment; after the fifth, Pub/Sub publishes it to payments-dead.
