retry_after(delay) holds the delivery under its lease for the delay, then nacks it, so the subscription redelivers it once the delay is over. Pub/Sub has no delayed nack, so the crate keeps the delivery in the process for the delay. The client goes on extending the delivery's lease while it waits, so the service does not redeliver it early. The wait runs on a task of its own, and the subscription keeps delivering meanwhile. The held delivery counts toward max_outstanding until it comes back, and its redelivery counts as an attempt toward a dead-letter policy. Nothing is published: the message itself comes back, with its payload and its attributes, and with the next attempt number where the subscription counts attempts. The delay must fit inside the subscription's max_lease, an hour by default. A longer one is refused with PubSubError::DelayBeyondLease, and the delivery comes back at once. A process that stops while it holds a delivery stops extending its lease, and the service redelivers the message when the lease runs out: the delay is lost, the message is not.

A payment the bank has not settled yet comes back in thirty seconds. The test advances the paused clock and sees the second delivery only once the thirty seconds are over. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_settlement_retry_after.rs /// A payment the bank has not settled yet comes back in thirty seconds, not at once. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("payments-workers").create_with_topic("payments"))] async fn reconcile(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { if !payment.settled { return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment reconciled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_settlement_retry_after.rs /// A payment the bank has not settled yet comes back in thirty seconds, not at once. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<Payment> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if !payment.settled { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment reconciled"); ready(Ok(())) } }

A name in #[subscriber] reads that existing Pub/Sub subscription; the GooglePubSub descriptor carries every other setting of one. Pub/Sub keeps topics and subscriptions apart. A publisher sends to a topic, and a subscription attached to the topic keeps every message published after it was created. Each subscription of a topic receives every message, and the consumers of one subscription share its messages. A service reads a subscription, never a topic. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] reads the subscription orders-workers, which the deployment created on its topic. The name is a short id in the broker's project or a full resource name, projects/{project}/subscriptions/{id}. Nothing is created at startup, and a subscription that does not exist fails on its stream with PubSubError::Receive. A dead-letter declaration at the mount site reaches a subscription named this way too. Every other setting belongs to the descriptor, which goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, body), and a descriptor goes in the same place, subscriber(descriptor, body). Two handlers on one subscription are two consumers of it: each message goes to one of them.

The subscription orders-workers of the project my-project. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions.rs /// Reads the subscription `orders-workers`, which the deployment created on its topic. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(place); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions.rs /// Reads the subscription `orders-workers`, which the deployment created on its topic. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders-workers", Place).build()); }, ) }

ack_extension sets how far each background extension of a delivery's lease reaches, from 10 seconds to 10 minutes, 60 seconds by default. Pub/Sub redelivers a message whose ack deadline passes before it is settled. While a handler works, the client library extends that deadline in the background, each time by this much. A longer extension means fewer calls for a slow handler. A shorter one brings a delivery back sooner when the process dies, because the service redelivers once the last extension runs out. The client clamps the value to the 10 seconds to 10 minutes Pub/Sub accepts. It is independent of the ack deadline configured on the subscription. How long the client keeps extending one delivery is max_lease.

A report takes minutes to render, so each extension reaches five minutes. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// A report takes minutes to render, so each extension of its lease reaches five minutes. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("flow-reports-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-reports") .ack_extension(Duration::from_mins(5)) )] async fn render(report: &Report) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(report.id, "report rendered"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// A report takes minutes to render, so each extension of its lease reaches five minutes. fn reports() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("flow-reports-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-reports") .ack_extension(Duration::from_mins(5)) }

A slice handler takes batches assembled on the client: batch(n) bounds their size, and batch_wait the wait for a partial one. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. The streaming pull hands over one delivery at a time, so the subscription gathers deliveries into a batch itself. A batch goes to the handler when it holds n deliveries, or when batch_wait has passed since its first one, 50 milliseconds by default. So a quiet subscription yields small batches, and a busy one full ones. One outcome settles every delivery of the batch; a Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles delivery i with outcome i. Every delivery of a batch is outstanding while the batch waits, so max_outstanding below n keeps batches short of n. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles delivery by delivery.

Three orders published together arrive in one call. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_batches.rs /// The slice makes this a batch handler; a partial batch waits 200 milliseconds for the rest. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(200)))] async fn settle(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // At most 50 orders reach the handler per call. b.include(settle.batch(nonzero!(50))); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_batches.rs /// The slice makes this a batch handler; a partial batch waits 200 milliseconds for the rest. struct Settle; impl Handle<[Order]> for Settle { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders settled"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // At most 50 orders reach the handler per call. b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(200)), Settle, ) .batch(nonzero!(50)) .build(), ); }, ) }

create_with_topic creates the subscription and its topic at startup where they are missing, with message ordering on. At startup the subscription looks the topic up and creates it when it is missing. It does the same for the declared dead-letter topic, and then for the subscription itself, attached to the topic. A subscription it creates has message ordering on and carries the declared dead-letter policy. A subscription that already exists keeps its own configuration; the crate changes only its dead-letter policy, where the mount site declared one. The calls need the permissions to create topics and subscriptions, which a production service often lacks. So the step suits the emulator, tests and services that own their topology; elsewhere the topology is infrastructure and the descriptor only names it. Several subscriptions created on one topic each receive every message published to it.

Two subscriptions on the topic orders: each receives every order. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` on the topic `orders`, with at most 100 orders unsettled. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers") .create_with_topic("orders") .max_outstanding(100) )] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// A second subscription on the same topic: it receives every order too. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-audit").create_with_topic("orders"))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` on the topic `orders`, with at most 100 orders unsettled. fn orders() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers") .create_with_topic("orders") .max_outstanding(100) } /// A second subscription on the same topic: it receives every order too. fn audit() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("orders-audit").create_with_topic("orders") }

GooglePubSub names one subscription by short id or full resource name and carries its settings: topology, flow control, leases and batches. GooglePubSub::new takes the subscription's name, and builder steps add the rest. create_with_topic creates the subscription and its topic at startup. max_outstanding caps the deliveries that may be unsettled at once. ack_extension and max_lease shape how the client keeps a delivery leased. batch_wait bounds how long a partial batch waits for the rest. A setting the descriptor leaves out keeps the client library's default. The descriptor is plain data and holds no connection. It opens against the connected broker at startup, so the declaration a service ships is the one its tests run.

The subscription orders-workers on the topic orders, with at most 100 orders unsettled at once. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` on the topic `orders`, with at most 100 orders unsettled. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers") .create_with_topic("orders") .max_outstanding(100) )] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` on the topic `orders`, with at most 100 orders unsettled. fn orders() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers") .create_with_topic("orders") .max_outstanding(100) }

max_lease is how long the client keeps extending the lease of one unsettled delivery, an hour by default, and the budget of retry_after. After a delivery has been held this long, the client stops extending its lease. The lease then runs out, and Pub/Sub redelivers the message, possibly to another consumer. A handler that may run longer than an hour needs a longer lease. retry_after(delay) holds the delivery in the process for the delay, under this same lease. A delay longer than max_lease is refused with PubSubError::DelayBeyondLease, and the delivery comes back at once. The refusal keeps the delivery from coming back before the delay is over, from a lease that ran out.

An invoice that is not ready comes back in ninety minutes, inside a lease of two hours. The tests advance the clock past the ninety minutes, and show that a delay of three hours comes back at once. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// An invoice that is not ready comes back in ninety minutes, inside a lease of two hours. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("flow-invoices-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-invoices") .max_lease(Duration::from_hours(2)) )] async fn send(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { if !invoice.ready { return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(NOT_READY); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// An invoice that is not ready comes back in ninety minutes, inside a lease of two hours. struct Send; impl Handle<Invoice> for Send { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if !invoice.ready { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(NOT_READY))); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice sent"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn invoices() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("flow-invoices-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-invoices") .max_lease(Duration::from_hours(2)) }

max_outstanding caps how many deliveries may be unsettled at once; Pub/Sub stops sending at the cap and resumes below it. A delivery is outstanding from the moment the service receives it until a handler settles it. The limit travels with the streaming pull, and the service holds the stream to it. It applies to one stream, not to the subscription as a whole: two instances of the service each hold their own share. The default is the client library's 1000 messages; a value of zero or less sets no limit. A delivery held by retry_after stays outstanding until it comes back. The client also caps outstanding bytes at 100 MiB, a limit the descriptor leaves at its default.

At most 50 orders are unsettled at once. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// At most 50 orders are unsettled at once; the service holds the rest back. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("flow-orders-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-orders") .max_outstanding(50) )] async fn index(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order indexed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// At most 50 orders are unsettled at once; the service holds the rest back. fn orders() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("flow-orders-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-orders") .max_outstanding(50) }

#[subscriber(GooglePubSub)] fixes the kind of subscription, and name at the mount site leaves its name to the deployment. A handler written with the bare kind has no subscription yet. .name("orders-workers") where it is mounted builds the descriptor, as GooglePubSub::new would. A definition mounted without a name does not compile. The descriptor built this way keeps every default; a subscription with settings of its own is a descriptor in the attribute. The same handler serves several deployments that each read a subscription of their own, such as one per region. The manual form starts from Unnamed::<GooglePubSub>::new() and takes the same .name(..) step.

Each deployment names its subscription in ORDERS_SUBSCRIPTION. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_name.rs /// A Pub/Sub subscription whose name the deployment decides. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub)] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// One service per region, each reading the subscription of its region. fn service(subscription: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(place.name(subscription)); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_name.rs /// A Pub/Sub subscription whose name the deployment decides. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// One service per region, each reading the subscription of its region. fn service(subscription: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<GooglePubSub>::new(), Place) .name(subscription) .build(), ); }, ) }

TestApp::start connects PubSubBroker in process: topics, subscriptions, redelivery and dead letters, with no emulator. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. Nothing is dialled and no credentials are read, so a test runs where the service could not authenticate. The in-process mode keeps Pub/Sub's model. A topic and a subscription are separate, and a subscription receives every message published to its topic after it was created, whether or not a consumer is open. A subscription the service only names is taken to exist, attached to the topic of its own name; create_with_topic attaches one to the topic it names. The consumers of one subscription share its messages in turn. A nack redelivers, a retry_after waits on the test's clock, and a dead-letter policy counts attempts and moves a spent message. It refuses what the service refuses: a resource name it does not accept, an empty message, an attribute or an ordering key past its limits or not UTF-8. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled. With tokio::time::pause(), or #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)], tb.advance(d) moves the clock and runs what fell due. Leases, flow control, ordered delivery by key and exactly-once delivery belong to the service; a live test checks them against the emulator.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-gcp-pubsub = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } The first test publishes a payment and reads how the handler settled it. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_settled_payment_is_charged() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let payment = Payment { id: 7, amount_cents: 1_000, settled: true, }; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&payment) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("payments-workers") .assert_called_once() .with(&payment) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } examples/manual/pubsub_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_settled_payment_is_charged() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let payment = Payment { id: 7, amount_cents: 1_000, settled: true, }; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&payment) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("payments-workers") .assert_called_once() .with(&payment) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } A payment the bank never settles comes back every thirty seconds and is dead-lettered after its fifth attempt. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_testing.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn an_unsettled_payment_is_dead_lettered_after_five_attempts() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let payment = Payment { id: 8, amount_cents: 1_000, settled: false, }; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&payment) .publish() .await?; for _ in 0..5 { tb.advance(RECHECK).await?; } tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("payments-workers") .assert_called(5); tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .published::<Payment>("payments-dead") .assert_called_once() .with(&payment); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } examples/manual/pubsub_testing.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn an_unsettled_payment_is_dead_lettered_after_five_attempts() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let payment = Payment { id: 8, amount_cents: 1_000, settled: false, }; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&payment) .publish() .await?; for _ in 0..5 { tb.advance(RECHECK).await?; } tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("payments-workers") .assert_called(5); tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .published::<Payment>("payments-dead") .assert_called_once() .with(&payment); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) }

TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against the Pub/Sub emulator, for leases, flow control and ordered delivery. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so every subscription opens a real streaming pull. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live app is the production one on a broker pointed at the emulator. The emulator starts empty, so its subscriptions create themselves with create_with_topic. It keeps its subscriptions until it stops, so a run that failed can leave messages behind for the next one. The examples delete their subscriptions before each live run, which live::fresh does with the client library's admin API. In the example, live::host returns the emulator's address from PUBSUB_TEST_HOST, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no emulator. A job that stood an emulator up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the emulator at PUBSUB_TEST_HOST. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_testing_live.rs /// The body both modes run; only the start call differs. async fn accepts_a_payment(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("testing-live-payments-workers") .assert_called_once() .with(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { accepts_a_payment(TestApp::start(app()).await?).await } #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn against_the_emulator() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(host) = live::host() else { return Ok(()); }; live::fresh(&host, &["testing-live-payments-workers"]).await?; let broker = PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator(host); accepts_a_payment(TestApp::start_live(service(broker)).await?).await } examples/manual/pubsub_testing_live.rs /// The body both modes run; only the start call differs. async fn accepts_a_payment(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("testing-live-payments-workers") .assert_called_once() .with(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { accepts_a_payment(TestApp::start(app()).await?).await } #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn against_the_emulator() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(host) = live::host() else { return Ok(()); }; live::fresh(&host, &["testing-live-payments-workers"]).await?; let broker = PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator(host); accepts_a_payment(TestApp::start_live(service(broker)).await?).await }

This guide hands a handler many messages at once, for work that is cheaper per batch than per message, such as one write to a warehouse. Pub/Sub delivers messages one by one and settles each on its own. The service collects the deliveries of one subscription into a batch on its side, calls the handler once for the batch, and then settles every message of it. The example loads page clicks into an analytics warehouse.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Loads a batch of clicks into the warehouse in one write. A click from a user the warehouse /// does not know yet comes back on its own; a click without a page is dropped. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("clicks-loader") .create_with_topic("clicks") .batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(500)) )] async fn load(clicks: &[Click]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { tracing::info!(count = clicks.len(), "clicks loaded"); clicks.iter().map(settle).collect() } fn settle(click: &Click) -> HandlerOutcome { if click.page.is_empty() { HandlerOutcome::drop() } else if click.user == UNKNOWN_USER { HandlerOutcome::retry() } else { HandlerOutcome::ack() } } src/main.rs /// Loads a batch of clicks into the warehouse in one write. A click from a user the warehouse /// does not know yet comes back on its own; a click without a page is dropped. struct Load; impl Handle<[Click]> for Load { fn handle( &self, clicks: &[Click], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = clicks.len(), "clicks loaded"); // `Err` carries one outcome per click, in the order of the batch. ready(Err(clicks.iter().map(settle).collect())) } } fn settle(click: &Click) -> HandlerOutcome { if click.page.is_empty() { HandlerOutcome::drop() } else if click.user == UNKNOWN_USER { HandlerOutcome::retry() } else { HandlerOutcome::ack() } } A slice parameter, &[Click], makes load a batch handler. batch_wait on the descriptor is how long a batch short of its size waits for more messages, half a second here. A batch is handed over as soon as it is full, or when the wait is over with what it has. load returns one outcome per click, in the order of the batch. A click from a user the warehouse does not know yet is retried: Pub/Sub delivers that click again, and it arrives on its own or in a later batch. A click without a page is dropped, and the rest are acknowledged. A single HandlerOutcome settles the whole batch the same way. In the manual form Ok(()) acknowledges the batch, and Err carries the outcomes click by click.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("clicks", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085"), |b| { // At most a hundred clicks per call; a click refused five times goes to `clicks-dead`. b.include(load.batch(nonzero!(100))) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("clicks-dead"); }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("clicks", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085"), |b| { // At most a hundred clicks per call; a click refused five times goes to `clicks-dead`. b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("clicks-loader") .create_with_topic("clicks") .batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(500)), Load, ) .batch(nonzero!(100)) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("clicks-dead"); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } batch(nonzero!(100)) is the batch size, and a batch handler does not compile without it. Every message of a batch is leased until the batch is settled, so the batch size stays under the subscription's max_outstanding, 1000 by default. The dead-letter declaration counts each click on its own: after five deliveries a click goes to clicks-dead, however many batches it rode in. Acknowledgement and retries covers the dead-letter topic.

The tests publish clicks together with tokio::join!, so they meet in one batch, and read the batches back with assert_batch_sizes and batches. A retried click shows up as a batch of one: the batch of two, then the stranger's click alone four more times, and then it is on clicks-dead. Testing a Pub/Sub service covers the harness.

This guide bounds how many messages a subscription holds at once and keeps a slow message leased while the service works on it or waits for it. Pub/Sub leases each message it delivers on a streaming pull. While the lease lasts, the subscription does not deliver the message to anyone else. The client extends the lease in the background until the message is settled, up to a limit. A lease that runs out sends the message to another consumer, even if the first one is still working on it. The example is a reports service: rendering a report takes a while, and sometimes its data is not there yet.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long a report whose data is late waits before it is tried again. const DATA_LATE: Duration = Duration::from_secs(20); #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("reports-renderer") .create_with_topic("reports") .max_outstanding(10) .ack_extension(Duration::from_mins(1)) .max_lease(Duration::from_mins(30)) )] async fn render(request: &ReportRequest) -> HandlerOutcome { if !request.data_ready { tracing::info!(request.id, "report data late, report held"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(DATA_LATE); } tracing::info!(request.id, "report rendered"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// How long a report whose data is late waits before it is tried again. const DATA_LATE: Duration = Duration::from_secs(20); struct Render; impl Handle<ReportRequest> for Render { fn handle( &self, request: &ReportRequest, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if !request.data_ready { tracing::info!(request.id, "report data late, report held"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(DATA_LATE))); } tracing::info!(request.id, "report rendered"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn reports() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("reports-renderer") .create_with_topic("reports") .max_outstanding(10) .ack_extension(Duration::from_mins(1)) .max_lease(Duration::from_mins(30)) } All three settings are steps of the GooglePubSub descriptor. max_outstanding(10) caps the messages the service holds unsettled at once. At the cap Pub/Sub stops sending, and it resumes as messages are settled. A message held by retry_after counts toward the cap until it comes back. The client's default is 1000; a small cap keeps slow work from piling up in one replica while others are idle. ack_extension is how far each extension of a lease reaches, a minute here. The client keeps it between 10 seconds and 10 minutes. A longer extension means fewer calls to Pub/Sub; a shorter one hands a message to another consumer sooner after a replica dies. max_lease is how long the client goes on extending one lease, 30 minutes here and an hour by default. It is also the longest delay a retry_after may ask for: the delay is spent under the lease.

render asks for a report whose data is late again in 20 seconds, with retry_after. The service keeps the message for the delay and the client extends its lease, so no other consumer gets it meanwhile. When the delay is over the service nacks the message, and Pub/Sub delivers it again. A delay longer than max_lease would outlive the lease, so the service refuses it and the message comes back at once. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The service on `broker`; `app` runs it against the local emulator. fn service(broker: PubSubBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(render); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085")) } src/main.rs /// The service on `broker`; `app` runs it against the local emulator. fn service(broker: PubSubBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(reports(), Render).build()); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085")) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The app is built by service(broker), so a test runs the same service in process and against the emulator.

The test publishes a report whose data is late and checks that it comes back once, after the 20 seconds. In process the delay passes on a paused clock. The in-process Pub/Sub has no leases and no flow control, so the same test also runs against the emulator, where the 20 seconds are real. There the wait is twice the subscription's 10-second acknowledgement deadline, and the report comes back only once: the lease held it. docker compose up -d PUBSUB_TEST_HOST=localhost:8085 cargo test -- --test-threads=1 The live test reads the emulator's address from PUBSUB_TEST_HOST and skips when it is unset. Testing a Pub/Sub service shows how one test body runs in both modes.
This guide installs ruststream-gcp-pubsub, starts the Pub/Sub emulator and runs a first service against it.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "json", "logging"] } ruststream-gcp-pubsub = "0.7" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-gcp-pubsub = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the default codec, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-gcp-pubsub is the Pub/Sub broker. Its testing feature adds the in-process Pub/Sub that tests run on. The broker crate has two features, both off by default: Feature What it gives testing the in-process Pub/Sub behind TestApp asyncapi the Pub/Sub bindings in the generated AsyncAPI document The client underneath is google-cloud-pubsub, written in Rust, so the build needs no system libraries. The crate needs Rust 1.95 or newer.

Google ships a Pub/Sub emulator in the Cloud SDK image: compose.yaml services: pubsub: image: gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:emulators command: gcloud beta emulators pubsub start --host-port=0.0.0.0:8085 --project=my-project ports: - "8085:8085" docker compose up -d The emulator listens on localhost:8085. It starts empty and accepts any project id.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").create_with_topic("orders"))] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085"), |b| { b.include(take_order); }, ) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085"), |b| { b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").create_with_topic("orders"), TakeOrder, ) .build(), ); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } take_order reads JSON orders from the subscription orders-workers. It takes an order with an amount and drops one without. A Pub/Sub service reads a subscription, never a topic. GooglePubSub describes the subscription, and create_with_topic creates it at startup on the topic orders, with the topic itself. PubSubBroker::new takes the project id and only records it. emulator points the broker at the local emulator, because the Rust client does not read PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST. The connection opens when the service starts. #[ruststream::app] turns app into main; in the manual form, run_main does the same. Run the service: cargo run -- run Publish an order from another terminal, through the emulator's REST API: curl -X POST localhost:8085/v1/projects/my-project/topics/orders:publish \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d "{\"messages\": [{\"data\": \"$(printf '{"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}' | base64)\"}]}" Pub/Sub carries the message body as base64 in its REST API, so the order is encoded first. The service logs order taken with the order's id. Ctrl+C stops it.

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, publishes an order and checks how take_order settled it. PubSubBroker connects to an in-process Pub/Sub there, so the tests need no emulator: cargo test Testing a Pub/Sub service walks through such tests and what the in-process Pub/Sub models.

A service on google-cloud-pubsub builds its clients, pulls in a loop and publishes by hand. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: google-cloud-pubsub RustStream Subscriber::builder() with with_endpoint and with_credentials PubSubBroker::new, with endpoint, credentials or emulator subscriber.subscribe(name) and a loop over the message stream a #[subscriber(..)] handler set_max_outstanding_messages, set_max_lease_extension, set_max_lease max_outstanding, ack_extension, max_lease on the descriptor (Flow control and leases) create_topic and create_subscription on the admin clients create_with_topic (Topics and subscriptions) serde_json::from_slice over the message data the handler's parameter type, decoded by the codec handler.ack(), handler.nack() the handler's outcome: ack, retry, retry_after, drop (Acknowledgement and retries) Publisher::publish a reply or an Out parameter, sent through the Publish policy (Publishing and replies) Message::set_ordering_key the ordering_key step (Ordering keys)

This guide keeps the messages of one key in order: on the way in, through the service's own concurrency, and on the way out. Pub/Sub delivers messages in no particular order by default. A message published with an ordering key, to a subscription with message ordering on, arrives after every earlier message of the same key. Messages of different keys still arrive in any order, and that is what lets them be handled side by side. The guarantee holds for messages published to one region. The example is a ledger service: an entry changes the balance of one account, and the entries of one account must apply in order. The account service publishes each entry with the account's id as its ordering key.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The entries of one account reach one lane in publish order; eight lanes run side by side. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("ledger-posting").create_with_topic("ledger"), workers(8, by_key) )] async fn post( entry: &Entry, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher<Options = PubSubPublishOptions>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let posted = Posted { account: entry.account.clone(), amount_cents: entry.amount_cents, }; let sent = out .message(&posted) .to("postings") .ordering_key(entry.account.clone()) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(entry.account, error = %err, "posting not published, entry retried"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } src/main.rs /// Posts an entry and publishes the posting under the account's key. struct Post; impl<Slot> Handle<Entry, (), Outs<(Slot,)>> for Post where Slot: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher<Options = PubSubPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, outs: &Outs<(Slot,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let posted = Posted { account: entry.account.clone(), amount_cents: entry.amount_cents, }; let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&posted) .to("postings") .ordering_key(entry.account.clone()) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(entry.account, error = %err, "posting not published, entry retried"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } create_with_topic creates ledger-posting with message ordering on. Pub/Sub fixes that setting when the subscription is created, so a subscription operations own has it only if they turned it on. workers(8, by_key) handles up to eight entries at once in eight lanes. Every entry of one account goes to the same lane, and a lane handles its entries one after another. So the accounts are posted side by side, and the entries of one account keep their order. A delivery reports its ordering key in the partition-key header, which is the key the lanes read. In the manual form the lanes are the workers_by_key step of the chain. When a delivery of one key is redelivered, Pub/Sub delivers the later messages of that key again too, so a handler of an ordered subscription is idempotent.

post publishes the posted entry to postings under the account's key, named on the call with the ordering_key step. The step comes with the prelude, and it needs the Out parameter to name the crate's settings type, Publisher<Options = PubSubPublishOptions>. A publish without a key carries no ordering. A reply has no call to name a key on. A publish transform sets it per delivery: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "statements")] struct Statement { account: String, amount_cents: i64, } /// Answers each entry with a statement line for the account's owner. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("ledger-statements").create_with_topic("ledger"), reply)] async fn notify(entry: &Entry) -> Statement { Statement { account: entry.account.clone(), amount_cents: entry.amount_cents, } } /// Sends each reply under the key of the entry it answers, which the delivery reports in its /// `partition-key` header. struct UnderTheEntrysKey; impl<C> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, PubSubPublishOptions> for UnderTheEntrysKey { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, _out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, options: &mut Option<PubSubPublishOptions>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(key) = cx.headers().get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) { options .get_or_insert_with(PubSubPublishOptions::default) .ordering_key = Some(key.to_owned()); } } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "statements")] struct Statement { account: String, amount_cents: i64, } /// Answers each entry with a statement line for the account's owner. struct Notify; impl Handle<Entry, Statement> for Notify { fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Statement, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Statement { account: entry.account.clone(), amount_cents: entry.amount_cents, })) } } /// Sends each reply under the key of the entry it answers, which the delivery reports in its /// `partition-key` header. struct UnderTheEntrysKey; impl<C> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, PubSubPublishOptions> for UnderTheEntrysKey { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, _out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, options: &mut Option<PubSubPublishOptions>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(key) = cx.headers().get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) { options .get_or_insert_with(PubSubPublishOptions::default) .ordering_key = Some(key.to_owned()); } } } UnderTheEntrysKey reads the key the entry arrived with and gives it to the statement, so the statements of one account stay in order too. A key that is the same for every message of a mount site goes on the policy instead: Publish::default().ordering_key(..). Where several name one, the call wins over the partition-key header, and the header over the policy. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085"), |b| { b.include(post).out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()).build(); b.include(notify) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(UnderTheEntrysKey); }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085"), |b| { // The entries of one account reach one lane in publish order; eight lanes run side // by side. b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("ledger-posting").create_with_topic("ledger"), Post, ) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(8)) .build(), ) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("ledger-statements").create_with_topic("ledger"), Notify, ) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(UnderTheEntrysKey); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } A failed publish with a key pauses that key in the client; the crate resumes it, so the next publish of the key goes out, and the failure reaches the handler as an error. Against the emulator, create the topics postings and statements before the service starts, as in Publishing and replies.
documents.s: The key on what the service publishes

documents.t: The tests publish an entry with the account's key in the partition-key header, the way the account service's key reaches a delivery. They check the key on the posting with tb.out::<DefaultSlot>().with_options(..), and on the statement with published(..).with_options(..). The in-process Pub/Sub does not model ordered delivery; the ordering component page holds a test of it against the emulator.

This guide takes a service from the emulator to Google Cloud: how it signs in, which endpoint it reaches, who owns the topology and which roles it needs. The example is a payments service configured from its environment.

src/main.rs /// Where the service runs, read from its environment. struct Config { project: String, /// A locational endpoint, such as `https://us-east1-pubsub.googleapis.com`. endpoint: Option<String>, } impl Config { fn from_env() -> Self { Self { project: env::var("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT") .expect("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT names the project"), endpoint: env::var("PUBSUB_ENDPOINT").ok(), } } } /// Application Default Credentials, and the endpoint the deployment names, if any. fn broker(config: Config) -> PubSubBroker { let broker = PubSubBroker::new(config.project); match config.endpoint { Some(endpoint) => broker.endpoint(endpoint), None => broker, } } Without emulator, the broker reaches Google Cloud. It signs in with Application Default Credentials, so the code names no credentials. On GKE, Cloud Run and Compute Engine they come from the metadata server: the service runs as the service account of its workload. On a developer machine gcloud auth application-default login writes them, and GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS names a key file anywhere else. A service that must sign in as a particular account builds a credentials value with google-cloud-auth and passes it to credentials. The clients ask for a token on their first call to Pub/Sub, so wrong credentials show up as the error of that call: a topology call at startup, a subscription's stream or a publish. The global endpoint routes each request to a nearby region. endpoint pins the service to one region, here from PUBSUB_ENDPOINT. Two guarantees need that: messages of one ordering key arrive in order only when they are published to one region, and an exactly-once subscription delivers once only to subscribers in its own region. The endpoint applies to every client of the broker, the startup's topology calls included.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// A subscription operations created on the topic `payments`. #[subscriber("payments-workers")] async fn charge(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "payment without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(payment.id, payment.amount_cents, "payment charged"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(config: Config) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker(config), |b| { // Written onto the subscription at startup, which needs `pubsub.subscriptions.update`. b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments-dead"); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(Config::from_env()) } src/main.rs /// Charges a payment read from a subscription operations created on the topic `payments`. struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if payment.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "payment without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(payment.id, payment.amount_cents, "payment charged"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(config: Config) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker(config), |b| { // Written onto the subscription at startup, which needs `pubsub.subscriptions.update`. b.include(subscriber("payments-workers", Charge).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments-dead"); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(Config::from_env()) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } In production the topics and subscriptions are usually infrastructure, created by Terraform or gcloud with their retention, filters and retry policy. The service then names its subscription, #[subscriber("payments-workers")], and creates nothing. The dead-letter declaration still applies: at startup the service writes it onto the subscription as its dead-letter policy. To keep the policy with the infrastructure as well, operations set the same cap and topic, and the update at startup changes nothing. create_with_topic suits a service that owns its topology, and the emulator. Startup stops at the first topology call Pub/Sub refuses, with PubSubError::Admin naming the resource. A subscription that is not there fails on its stream with PubSubError::Receive.

The service account of the service needs these permissions: The service Permissions Predefined role reads a subscription pubsub.subscriptions.consume on it roles/pubsub.subscriber publishes to a topic pubsub.topics.publish on it roles/pubsub.publisher declares a dead-letter policy on a subscription pubsub.subscriptions.update on it roles/pubsub.editor uses create_with_topic pubsub.topics.get, pubsub.topics.create, pubsub.topics.attachSubscription, pubsub.subscriptions.get, pubsub.subscriptions.create in the project roles/pubsub.editor A dead-letter policy also needs the Pub/Sub service agent of the project, service-{project-number}@gcp-sa-pubsub.iam.gserviceaccount.com. It publishes to the dead-letter topic, so it needs roles/pubsub.publisher there, and it acknowledges the moved message, so it needs roles/pubsub.subscriber on the source subscription.

Exactly-once is a setting of the subscription, made by operations when they create it. The crate needs no setting: on such a subscription each acknowledgement waits for Pub/Sub to confirm it, and one Pub/Sub rejects fails with an error that names the cause. The service connects through the regional endpoint of the subscription's region, because the guarantee holds there only. Acknowledgement and retries covers what changes for a handler.

The tests start the same service with a Config of their own, in process, where nothing is dialled and no credentials are read. app reads the environment, so main fails at once without GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT, before any connection.

This guide publishes to Pub/Sub topics in the three ways a service does: a reply to a message, a publish from inside a handler, and a message once the service is up. Every publish goes through a publish policy. Publish, the prelude's name for PubSubPublish, publishes to a topic and waits for the service to accept the message. A topic that does not exist fails the publish: Pub/Sub keeps no message for a topic it does not have. The example is an orders service that answers each order with a receipt, bills it, and announces that it is up.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The receipt of an order; its type names the topic it goes to. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-receipts").create_with_topic("orders"), reply)] async fn receipt(order: &Order) -> Receipt { tracing::info!(order.id, "receipt sent"); Receipt { order_id: order.id } } src/main.rs /// The receipt of an order; its type names the topic it goes to. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } struct ReceiptFor; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for ReceiptFor { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "receipt sent"); ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } The reply clause makes the return value a message to publish. Where it goes is a property of its type: #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] sends every Receipt to the topic receipts. The receipt is published after the handler returns and before the order is acknowledged, so a receipt that fails to publish leaves the order unacknowledged, and it comes back.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Invoice { order_id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } /// Publishes the invoice of an order to the topic the call names. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-billing").create_with_topic("orders"))] async fn bill(order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let invoice = Invoice { order_id: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, }; match out.message(&invoice).to("invoices").publish().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, error = %err, "invoice not published, order retried"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Invoice { order_id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } /// Publishes the invoice of an order to the topic the call names. struct Bill; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Bill where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let invoice = Invoice { order_id: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, }; let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&invoice) .to("invoices") .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(order.id, error = %err, "invoice not published, order retried"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } An Out parameter is a publisher the handler calls itself. bill names the topic on the call with .to("invoices") and decides what a failed publish means for the order. Here it asks for the order again with retry, so the invoice is not lost. A handler may publish any number of messages, to any topics, before it settles.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085"), |b| { b.include(receipt).out_reply(Publish::default()); b.include(bill).out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()).build(); b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { publisher .message(&Started { service: "orders".to_owned(), }) .publish() .await }); }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085"), |b| { b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("orders-receipts").create_with_topic("orders"), ReceiptFor, ) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish::default()); b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("orders-billing").create_with_topic("orders"), Bill, ) .build(), ) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { publisher .message(&Started { service: "orders".to_owned(), }) .publish() .await }); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } .out_reply(Publish::default()) gives the reply its policy, and .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) gives the Out parameter its own. A policy holds settings for every message of its position: Publish::default().ordering_key(..) is one. The broker creates one client publisher per topic, on the first publish to it, and every later publish to that topic reuses it. after_startup runs once every subscription is open. It receives a live publisher of the policy it names, here to announce the service on services. A hook that fails stops the startup, so a service that cannot announce itself does not run.

The topics the service publishes to belong to whoever reads them, so they exist before the service starts. Against the emulator, create them through its REST API: for topic in receipts invoices services; do curl -X PUT localhost:8085/v1/projects/my-project/topics/$topic done cargo run -- run Without services, the announcement fails and the service does not start.

The tests in the example file publish an order and assert on what reached receipts and invoices with published. A second test starts the app and finds the announcement on services. In process, every publish is recorded whether or not a subscription reads its topic. Testing a Pub/Sub service covers the harness.

This guide settles each Pub/Sub delivery by the handler's outcome, retries now or after a delay, and caps the deliveries with a dead-letter topic. Pub/Sub settles every message on its own. An acknowledged message is done; a message given back is delivered again, possibly to another consumer. The subscription counts the deliveries and moves a message that ran out of them to its dead-letter topic. The crate maps the handler's outcome onto these verbs, and the mount site's cap onto the subscription's dead-letter policy. The example is a payments service that charges cards through a bank.

The bank answers a charge in four ways, and each needs a different outcome. Charged is done: ack. Held means the bank reviews the payment, which takes a while: retry_after asks again in 30 seconds. Unreachable means the bank did not answer: retry asks again at once. Declined means the card is closed, and another try gets the same answer, so the payment is dropped. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long the bank's review of a held payment takes. const HOLD: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("payments-workers").create_with_topic("payments"))] async fn charge(payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let attempt = ctx .headers() .get_str(DELIVERY_ATTEMPT_HEADER) .unwrap_or("1"); match ask_the_bank(payment) { Answer::Charged => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Answer::Held => { tracing::info!( payment.id, attempt, "payment held by the bank, asked again later" ); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD) } Answer::Unreachable => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, attempt, "bank unreachable, payment retried"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } Answer::Declined => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "card declined, payment dropped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs /// How long the bank's review of a held payment takes. const HOLD: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let attempt = ctx .headers() .get_str(DELIVERY_ATTEMPT_HEADER) .unwrap_or("1"); let settled = match ask_the_bank(payment) { Answer::Charged => Ok(()), Answer::Held => { tracing::info!( payment.id, attempt, "payment held by the bank, asked again later" ); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)) } Answer::Unreachable => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, attempt, "bank unreachable, payment retried"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } Answer::Declined => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "card declined, payment dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } }; ready(settled) } } On Pub/Sub the outcomes become these calls: Outcome What Pub/Sub does ack acknowledges; the message is not delivered again retry nacks; the subscription delivers the message again retry_after(delay) the service holds the message under its lease for the delay, then nacks it drop acknowledges; on the last delivery the cap allows, nacks, so the message goes to the dead-letter topic A subscription with no retry policy delivers a nacked message again at once. A subscription with an exponential backoff policy, set by operations, waits first, and then retry waits too. Pub/Sub has no delayed nack, so retry_after keeps the message in the service. The client goes on extending its lease for the delay, and nacks it when the delay is over. The delay must fit inside the subscription's max_lease, an hour by default; a longer one comes back at once. A service that stops during the delay stops extending the lease, and the message comes back when the lease runs out. Flow control and leases covers the lease. DELIVERY_ATTEMPT_HEADER is the delivery's attempt number, the first delivery being 1. Pub/Sub counts attempts only on a subscription with a dead-letter policy, and its count is an estimate that may miss a delivery.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one payment, the first included; then `payments-dead`. b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments-dead"); b.include(review); }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator("localhost:8085"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one payment, the first included; then `payments-dead`. b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("payments-workers").create_with_topic("payments"), Charge, ) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments-dead"); b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("payments-dead-review").create_with_topic("payments-dead"), Review, ) .build(), ); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } max_attempts and dead_letter become the subscription's own dead-letter policy, written at startup. After the fifth delivery Pub/Sub stops delivering the payment and publishes it to payments-dead, payload and attributes as they arrived. The service publishes nothing itself, so a crash cannot lose the move. Pub/Sub accepts a cap from 5 to 100; anything else, or one half of the pair alone, fails the startup. A dropped payment is acknowledged and goes nowhere; the dead-letter topic holds only the payments that ran out of deliveries. The subscription payments-workers is created with the policy, and the topic payments-dead with it. A subscription operations created gets the policy written onto it at startup instead. In production the Pub/Sub service account of the project needs permission to publish to the dead-letter topic and to subscribe to the source subscription; Running in production lists the roles.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Reads the dead-letter topic through a subscription of its own. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("payments-dead-review").create_with_topic("payments-dead"))] async fn review(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!( payment.id, "payment ran out of attempts, a person looks at it" ); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Reads the dead-letter topic through a subscription of its own. struct Review; impl Handle<Payment> for Review { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::error!( payment.id, "payment ran out of attempts, a person looks at it" ); ready(Ok(())) } } The dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic, and review reads it through a subscription of its own. A message published to a topic with no subscription is lost, so the subscription exists before the first payment runs out of deliveries. Here review creates it at startup.

A subscription with exactly-once delivery on guarantees that an acknowledged message is not delivered again. It is a setting of the subscription, made when operations create it; the service needs no setting of its own. The crate reads it off each delivery, and on such a subscription ack and retry wait for Pub/Sub to confirm them. An acknowledgement Pub/Sub rejects, for example after the lease ran out, fails the settlement with an error that names the cause, and the message may come back. The guarantee holds for subscribers in the subscription's region, so the service connects through that region's endpoint.

The tests in the example file publish one payment per answer. A held payment comes back only once 30 seconds have passed on the paused clock. An unreachable bank costs five deliveries, and then review receives the payment. A declined payment is handled once and never reaches the review. Testing a Pub/Sub service covers the harness.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, against an in-process Pub/Sub or against the emulator. The service under test sends refunds. A refund arrives on refunds, and the handler answers it with a Refunded message on refunds-done. A refund without an amount is dropped. A refund above the approval limit waits a minute for approval with retry_after. After five deliveries a refund goes to refunds-review, the dead-letter topic. The app is built by service(broker), so a test chooses the broker and main uses the one for the emulator. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-gcp-pubsub in [dev-dependencies].

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The body both modes run: a refund is answered on `refunds-done`. async fn a_refund_is_answered(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&Refund { id: 7, amount_cents: 1250, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("refunds-workers") .assert_called_once() .with(&Refund { id: 7, amount_cents: 1250, }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .published::<Refunded>("refunds-done") .assert_called_once() .with(&Refunded { refund_id: 7 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { a_refund_is_answered(TestApp::start(app()).await?).await } src/main.rs /// The body both modes run: a refund is answered on `refunds-done`. async fn a_refund_is_answered(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&Refund { id: 7, amount_cents: 1250, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("refunds-workers") .assert_called_once() .with(&Refund { id: 7, amount_cents: 1250, }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .published::<Refunded>("refunds-done") .assert_called_once() .with(&Refunded { refund_id: 7 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { a_refund_is_answered(TestApp::start(app()).await?).await } TestApp::start connects PubSubBroker to an in-process Pub/Sub. Nothing is dialled and no credentials are read. The test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>(). Refund names its topic, so message(..).publish() needs no destination. publish returns once the handler and its reply have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscriber settled and what reached refunds-done. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the live test below runs it too.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_refund_without_an_amount_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&Refund { id: 8, amount_cents: 0, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("refunds-workers") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .published::<Refunded>("refunds-done") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_refund_without_an_amount_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&Refund { id: 8, amount_cents: 0, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("refunds-workers") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .published::<Refunded>("refunds-done") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } settled checks the outcome the handler returned. assert_not_called checks that no answer was published.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_refund_never_approved_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let large = Refund { id: 9, amount_cents: 250_000, }; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&large) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("refunds-workers") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(APPROVAL_WAIT)); // Each wait ends in a redelivery, and the fifth delivery is the last one allowed. for deliveries in 2..=5 { tb.advance(APPROVAL_WAIT).await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("refunds-workers") .assert_called(deliveries); } // The fifth delivery waits too; when its wait ends, Pub/Sub moves the refund to review. tb.advance(APPROVAL_WAIT).await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .published::<Refund>("refunds-review") .assert_called_once() .with(&large); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_refund_never_approved_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let large = Refund { id: 9, amount_cents: 250_000, }; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .message(&large) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("refunds-workers") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(APPROVAL_WAIT)); // Each wait ends in a redelivery, and the fifth delivery is the last one allowed. for deliveries in 2..=5 { tb.advance(APPROVAL_WAIT).await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .subscriber("refunds-workers") .assert_called(deliveries); } // The fifth delivery waits too; when its wait ends, Pub/Sub moves the refund to review. tb.advance(APPROVAL_WAIT).await?; tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>() .published::<Refund>("refunds-review") .assert_called_once() .with(&large); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } The test starts on a paused clock, and advance moves it forward. A minute of APPROVAL_WAIT costs nothing. Each wait ends in a redelivery of the same message, and assert_called counts them. The fifth delivery waits too, and when its wait ends Pub/Sub moves the refund to refunds-review as it arrived. published reads what reached a topic, whether the service or Pub/Sub put it there.

documents.t: The in-process Pub/Sub reads the production broker's project and every descriptor the service mounts. A publish, a subscription or a declaration Pub/Sub refuses fails the test the same way. It models Pub/Sub rather than a queue: Topics and subscriptions are separate, and each subscription of a topic receives every message published after it was created. The consumers of one subscription share its messages. retry delivers a message again, retry_after waits on the test's clock first, and drop acknowledges. A dead-letter policy counts the deliveries and moves a message that ran out of them. The topology the service expects to find is taken to exist. A subscription the service only names reads the topic of its own name, and a topic the service publishes to accepts the message. Leases, flow control, ordered delivery by key and exactly-once delivery need the emulator or Pub/Sub itself.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn against_the_emulator() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(host) = live::host() else { return Ok(()); }; live::fresh(&host, &["refunds-workers"]).await?; create_topic(&host, "refunds-done").await?; let broker = PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator(host); a_refund_is_answered(TestApp::start_live(service(broker)).await?).await } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn against_the_emulator() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(host) = live::host() else { return Ok(()); }; live::fresh(&host, &["refunds-workers"]).await?; create_topic(&host, "refunds-done").await?; let broker = PubSubBroker::new("my-project").emulator(host); a_refund_is_answered(TestApp::start_live(service(broker)).await?).await } TestApp::start_live connects the same app to the emulator. A publish then waits up to ten seconds for every subscription it reaches to handle it; start_live_within sets another deadline. The test reads the emulator's address from PUBSUB_TEST_HOST with live::host, a helper of the example's own, and skips when it is unset. The emulator keeps its subscriptions between runs, so live::fresh deletes refunds-workers first, and the run reads only what it publishes. create_topic creates refunds-done the way operations would, because a reply to a topic that is not there fails. The assertions are the in-process ones, unchanged. cargo test PUBSUB_TEST_HOST=localhost:8085 cargo test -- --test-threads=1
